What is an off-ramp in crypto? Meaning and steps

By the Ibanora teamPublished November 25, 20265 min read

In short

An off-ramp is a service that turns crypto or stablecoins into ordinary money, such as dollars or euros, and pays it out to a bank account, card or payment app. It is the reverse of an on-ramp. Exchanges, stablecoin issuers, card payments and apps with a built-in provider can all work as off-ramps.

The word comes from roads. Merriam-Webster defines an off-ramp as a ramp by which you leave a limited-access highway. So what is an off ramp in crypto? It is the way out of the blockchain: a service that buys your crypto or stablecoins and pays you ordinary money, for example into a bank account. You will also see it spelled "offramp".

What does off-ramp mean in crypto?

Official definitions describe the same activity in drier words. The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) lists "exchange between virtual assets and fiat currencies" among the activities that make a business a virtual asset service provider. Fiat currency is government-issued money, such as the US dollar or the euro.

The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) calls it "exchange of crypto-assets for funds". It defines the service as buying or selling crypto-assets with clients for funds, using the provider's own capital, and takes its meaning of funds from the EU Payment Services Directive (EU) 2015/2366. MiCA applies from December 30, 2024, with some parts applying earlier.

An off-ramp can take stablecoins as well as coins like bitcoin. MiCA calls a stablecoin that tracks one currency an e-money token: a crypto-asset that "purports to maintain a stable value by referencing the value of one official currency". When a cross-border payment travels as stablecoins and the recipient wants ordinary money, the last step is the job an off-ramp does: turning the stablecoins back into local currency.

How an off-ramp works, step by step

  1. Open an account with the provider and complete any checks it asks for.
  2. Move your tokens to the provider, or use a balance you already hold with it. On Ethereum, sending tokens from your own stablecoin wallet or crypto wallet costs a gas fee, paid in ether (ETH), according to ethereum.org.
  3. Ask for a quote: the amount of currency you will get for your tokens.
  4. Confirm the sale. Some providers buy your tokens with their own money; a trading platform matches you with another user instead. MiCA treats these as separate services.
  5. Receive the payout to a bank account, a card or another payment method the provider supports.

On-ramp vs off-ramp

An on-ramp makes the same trip in the other direction: ordinary money in, crypto out. The FATF wording covers both directions in one phrase, and MiCA's covers both purchase and sale. In an explainer dated July 17, 2025, Mastercard describes ramps as services that connect bank accounts, payment cards and digital wallets to crypto exchanges or platforms.

DirectionYou giveYou getWhere it ends up
On-rampMoney from a bank account, card or balanceCrypto or stablecoinsA crypto wallet
Off-rampCrypto or stablecoinsOrdinary moneyA bank account, card or payment app

Types of off-ramp

Selling on an exchange

You sell on the platform, then withdraw the money to your bank. US guidance from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) calls a business that swaps virtual currency for real currency an "exchanger".

Redeeming with the stablecoin issuer

A stablecoin has a second way out: the company that issued it can buy it back. Under Article 49 of MiCA, the issuer of an e-money token must redeem it at any time and at par value when a holder asks, paying in funds other than electronic money. MiCA also says the redemption must not carry a fee, with an exception tied to the issuer's recovery plan.

Direct redemption is not always open to everyone. As of November 2026, Circle says USDC is redeemable 1:1 for US dollars, and that its Circle Mint service lets exchanges, institutional traders, banks and large financial institutions redeem directly. Circle says Mint is not available to individuals or small businesses. It points startups and small businesses to on-ramp and off-ramp providers in its Circle Alliance Program, and individuals to exchanges, neobanks and digital wallets.

Spending with a card

Mastercard's July 2025 explainer also counts paying for goods priced in ordinary currency with crypto or stablecoins as an off-ramp, with the digital assets sent on to cards or bank accounts that hold ordinary money.

Off-ramp solutions inside other apps

Some wallets and apps offer cash-out through specialist ramp firms: the same Mastercard explainer names firms serving self-custodial wallet services, such as MoonPay and Transak.

Ibanora offers an on-ramp and off-ramp through its partner Mosta Payments Ltd. You can sell stablecoins for an ordinary currency and pay the proceeds out to a bank account, and the stablecoins and networks open to you depend on your country and verification. Businesses can talk to Ibanora about offering on-ramp and off-ramp to their own users.

What an off-ramp costs

The cost of cashing out can sit in more than one place. Questions to ask:

  • What network fee do I pay to send my tokens? On Ethereum, ethereum.org explains that the priority fee you add depends on network demand at the time: you may need to pay more when demand is high.
  • What rate does the quote use, and how far is it from the market rate?
  • Is there a separate fee for the sale or for the payout?
  • Does the payout involve a currency conversion, for example from a dollar stablecoin to euros?

The simplest test is the amount that lands in your account. For example, with made-up numbers that are not any provider's price: if you sell 1,000 dollar stablecoins, each worth $1, and receive $990, the off-ramp cost you $10, or 1%, however the provider splits it between rate and fees.

The rules off-ramps work under

In the US, FinCEN's guidance of March 18, 2013 says a person who uses virtual currency to buy goods or services is not a money services business. An exchanger that buys or sells convertible virtual currency for any reason is a money transmitter under FinCEN's rules, unless an exemption applies. Money transmitters are money services businesses, and FinCEN says that, with few exceptions, each money services business must register with the Department of the Treasury.

In the EU, MiCA defines a crypto-asset service provider as a business that is allowed to provide crypto-asset services under its Article 59. Exchanging crypto-assets for funds is one of those services.

What to check before you cash out

  • Can the provider serve you where you live? In the EU, look for a crypto-asset service provider under MiCA. In the US, FinCEN's guidance treats an exchanger that buys or sells convertible virtual currency as a money transmitter, unless an exemption applies, and FinCEN says most money services businesses must register with the Department of the Treasury.
  • Does it accept the exact token and network you hold?
  • Which bank accounts, cards or apps can it pay out to, and in which currencies?
  • What amount will land in your account after every charge?
  • Is the deposit address right? The Federal Trade Commission says cryptocurrency payments typically are not reversible.
  • Are you keeping records for tax? In the US, the IRS asks about digital asset sales on the federal tax return.

Questions

Is an off-ramp the same as a crypto exchange?

Not always. An exchange works as an off-ramp when it lets you sell and withdraw money, but MiCA lists running a trading platform and exchanging crypto-assets for funds as separate services. A card payment, an app with a built-in provider or the stablecoin issuer can also be your off-ramp.

Can a crypto off-ramp payment be reversed?

The crypto side usually cannot. The Federal Trade Commission says cryptocurrency payments typically are not reversible, and that you can usually only get your money back if the person you paid sends it back. Check the provider and the deposit address before you send.

Do I need to report an off-ramp sale for tax?

That depends on where you live. In the US, the IRS treats digital assets, including stablecoins, as property, not currency. The federal return asks whether you sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of a digital asset during the year, and brokers report certain sales on Form 1099-DA for transactions from January 1, 2025. A tax adviser can tell you how this applies to you.

What does off-ramp mean outside crypto?

On the road, an off-ramp is a ramp by which you leave a limited-access highway, according to Merriam-Webster. The dictionary dates the first known use of the word to 1939.
